# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams currently using Slack who are considering switching to Element, possibly due to concerns over data ownership or cost. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch would be to gain more control over data or to reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free for self-hosted deployments, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows full data ownership for self-hosted deployments, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but Element's self-hosted option provides more flexibility for large teams.
* Integration with external services: Slack has a more extensive library of integrations, including Google Drive and Trello, while Element supports integrations like GitHub and Jitsi.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Large library of integrations
* Good mobile app support
* Scalable for large teams
* Limited control over data storage
### Element
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Free for self-hosted deployments
* Highly customizable
* Supports end-to-end encryption
* Can be complex to set up and manage

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and have minimal concerns over data ownership. It's suitable for teams of all sizes, from small startups to large enterprises, and is particularly useful for those who need a wide range of integrations with external services. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for teams that require full control over their data and are comfortable with the technical requirements of self-hosting. This includes large organizations with strict data security policies and teams that need customized solutions.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides data in JSON format.
2. Set up an Element server, either on your own hardware or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Element import tool to migrate your Slack data to Element.
4. Configure any necessary integrations or customizations in Element.
5. Test your Element deployment to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its technical requirements and potential complexity. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's self-hosted option requires significant technical expertise to set up and manage. However, for teams that require full control over their data and are willing to invest in the setup and management, Element is a viable alternative to Slack.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need extensive integrations with external services
* Large organizations with strict data security policies
* Teams that require customized solutions and are comfortable with self-hosting
* Developers who need full control over their communication platform
* Teams that prioritize cost savings and do not need premium support

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Slack?
No, Slack does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is Element free?
Yes, Element is free for self-hosted deployments, but you will need to cover server costs.
### Can I migrate from Slack to Element?
Yes, you can migrate from Slack to Element using the Element import tool.
### Does Element support end-to-end encryption?
Yes, Element supports end-to-end encryption for all messages.
### Is Element suitable for large teams?
Yes, Element is scalable and suitable for large teams, but it requires more technical expertise to set up and manage.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. Both tools offer a core use case of facilitating real-time communication and collaboration among team members. The key reason someone would switch from Slack to Mattermost is to gain control over their data and reduce costs, as Mattermost offers a self-hosted option.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free self-hosted option, while Slack charges a per-user fee.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more user-friendly interface, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it a good option for large teams, while Slack's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost offers native integration with GitHub, while Slack requires a third-party integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Good mobile app support
* Limited control over data storage and security
* Can be expensive for large teams
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option gives teams full control over their data
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Good support for large teams and scalability
* Can be complex to set up and configure
* Limited support for certain third-party integrations

## When to Choose Each
### Slack
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, easy-to-use communication platform with a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. It's also a good option for teams that don't require a high level of control over their data storage and security.
### Mattermost
Mattermost is a good choice for large teams or organizations that require a high level of control over their data storage and security. It's also a good option for teams that need a highly customizable and extensible communication platform, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting it up and configuring it.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Mattermost using the Mattermost import tool.
4. Configure any necessary integrations with third-party apps.
5. Test your Mattermost setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for many teams, offering a high level of control over data storage and security. However, it's worth noting that Mattermost can be complex to set up and configure, and may require significant technical expertise. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile app support is not yet as robust as Slack's. We recommend switching to Mattermost if you're a large team or organization that requires a high level of control over your data storage and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting it up and configuring it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams that don't need a wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Teams that require a high level of control over their data storage and security
* Large teams that need a highly customizable and extensible communication platform
* Teams that are currently using Slack's free plan and need more features
* Teams that are looking to reduce their communication platform costs

## FAQ
### Can I use Mattermost for free?
Yes, Mattermost offers a free self-hosted option, as well as a free trial for its cloud-hosted option.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost can be more complex to set up and configure than Slack, especially for non-technical users.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with third-party apps?
Yes, Mattermost offers a wide range of integrations with third-party apps, although not as many as Slack.
### Can I use Mattermost on my mobile device?
Yes, Mattermost offers mobile apps for both iOS and Android, although they are not yet as robust as Slack's mobile apps.
### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Yes, Mattermost can be a good option for small teams, especially those that require a high level of control over their data storage and security.

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Obsidian is a free, self-hosted alternative to Notion. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms that help developers manage and collaborate on code. This comparison is beneficial for development teams, especially those considering switching from GitHub to GitLab due to concerns about data ownership or cost. The core use case for both platforms is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers a free plan with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, while GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitHub is generally easier to set up and use, especially for small teams, while GitLab requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: GitLab is more scalable than GitHub, especially for large teams and enterprises.
* Integration with CI/CD tools: GitLab has built-in CI/CD tools, while GitHub requires integration with third-party tools like Jenkins or CircleCI.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Free plan available
* Limited control over data
**GitLab:**
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Built-in CI/CD tools
* More scalable than GitHub
* Free self-hosted option
* Steeper learning curve due to more features

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is a good choice for small teams or individuals who want a simple, easy-to-use version control platform with a large community and ecosystem. It's also a good choice for teams that don't require full control over their data. GitLab, on the other hand, is a good choice for larger teams or enterprises that require more scalability and control over their data. It's also a good choice for teams that want to self-host their repositories and have built-in CI/CD tools.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub export tool, which exports data in a JSON file.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and import the JSON file using the GitLab import tool.
3. Update any references to the old GitHub repository in your code or documentation.
4. Test your code and ensure that everything is working as expected.
5. Delete your old GitHub repository.

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a wide range of features and scalability. However, one technical limitation to consider is the complexity of setting up and managing a self-hosted GitLab instance, which can be time-consuming and require significant technical expertise. Based on our analysis, we recommend switching to GitLab if you're a large team or enterprise that requires more control over your data and scalability, but if you're a small team or individual who wants a simple, easy-to-use platform, GitHub may still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (50+ users) that require more scalability and control over their data
* Enterprises that want to self-host their repositories for security and compliance reasons
* Teams that don't need GitHub's large community and ecosystem
* Developers who want built-in CI/CD tools and more features
* Organizations that require MIT (CE) licensing for their version control platform

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
Yes, GitLab offers a free self-hosted option, as well as a free plan with limited features on its cloud platform.
### Can I self-host GitHub?
No, GitHub does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is GitLab more secure than GitHub?
GitLab offers more security features, such as self-hosting and encryption, but both platforms have robust security measures in place.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to GitLab?
Yes, you can export your GitHub repository and import it into GitLab using the import tool.
### Does GitLab have a large community?
While GitLab's community is smaller than GitHub's, it is still active and growing, with many contributors and users.

comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced August 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Gitea is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and prototyping tools used by UI/UX designers, product managers, and developers. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals looking to switch from Figma to Penpot, primarily due to the core use case of collaborative design and the key reason of seeking a more cost-effective and self-hosted solution. The main difference between the two tools lies in their licensing, cost, and scalability.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Figma stores user data on its servers, whereas Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more streamlined and user-friendly setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed for large-scale teams and enterprises, whereas Penpot is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams and individuals.
* Feature Difference: Figma has a more comprehensive set of features, including advanced prototyping and collaboration tools, while Penpot has a more limited feature set but is highly customizable.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface and onboarding process
	+ Advanced features for prototyping and collaboration
	+ Large community and extensive plugin library
	+ Scalable and reliable infrastructure
	+ Excellent customer support
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over data ownership and storage
	+ Proprietary license with limited customization options
### Penpot
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source with self-hosting options
	+ Highly customizable and extensible
	+ Growing community and plugin library
	+ Suitable for small to medium-sized teams and individuals
	+ Cost-effective solution
* Cons:
	+ Limited features compared to Figma
	+ Steeper learning curve due to technical requirements
	+ Limited customer support and resources
	+ Still in active development with some stability issues

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams and enterprises that require advanced features, scalability, and reliability. It is also suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use and a user-friendly interface. On the other hand, Penpot is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, individuals, and organizations that value data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness. Penpot is also a good choice for teams that are comfortable with technical requirements and self-hosting.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in SVG or PNG format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs and convert them to Penpot's native format.
3. Configure your Penpot instance and set up user accounts and permissions.
4. Update your design files and collaborate with your team using Penpot's features.
5. Monitor your instance's performance and adjust settings as needed.

## Our Take
Penpot is still in active development and may not be production-ready for most users right now. While it shows great promise, it lacks the polish and stability of Figma. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Penpot's collaboration features are not yet as robust as Figma's. However, for teams that value data ownership, customization, and cost-effectiveness, Penpot is definitely worth considering. We recommend switching to Penpot if you are a small to medium-sized team or individual with basic design needs and a technical background.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need advanced features
* Individuals who value data ownership and self-hosting
* Organizations with limited budgets and basic design needs
* Teams that require high customization and extensibility
* Developers who want to integrate design tools with their existing infrastructure

## FAQ
### Is Penpot completely free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source, with no costs or licensing fees.
### Can I self-host Penpot?
Yes, Penpot allows self-hosting, giving you full control over your data and instance.
### Is Penpot as feature-rich as Figma?
No, Penpot has a more limited feature set compared to Figma, but it is highly customizable and extensible.
### Can I import my Figma designs into Penpot?
Yes, Penpot has an import tool that allows you to upload and convert your Figma designs.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams and enterprises?
Not yet, Penpot is still in active development and may not be production-ready for large teams and enterprises.
